unit.title: Prepare for oxyacetylene/metal arc welding processes

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before setting up for a structural weld, Dwayne reads the WPS (welding procedure specification). Which information does it give him?

essays.stem: Explain what a welding procedure specification (WPS) is, what it contains, and how a team leader uses the WPS and the welders' qualification records when preparing a coded job.
essays.modelAnswer: A WPS is a written set of instructions that tells the welder exactly how to make a weld so that it meets the code or specification. It is backed by a procedure qualification record (PQR), which shows that a test weld made that way passed its tests. The WPS gives the parent material and thickness range, the process, the joint design with bevel angle, root face, root gap and any backing, the welding positions, the filler or electrode type and size, the current, voltage, polarity and travel speed ranges, any shielding gas, preheat and interpass temperatures, the run sequence and any heat treatment after welding. The team leader gets the correct, current WPS for the job and makes sure the joints are prepared exactly to it, that the right consumables are issued and stored correctly, and that the machines can be set within its ranges. They check each welder's qualification record, so that only welders qualified for that process, position, material and thickness range weld the joints, and that their qualification is still in date. They keep the WPS at the work place and record what was used.
markingPoints: Defines the WPS and its link to a PQR
Lists the main contents (material, process, joint design, position, consumables, settings, preheat)
Leader makes sure preparation and consumables match the WPS
Checks welder qualifications for process, position, material and date
Keeps the WPS at the work place and records what was used

essays.stem: Explain the E7018 and E6013 classifications, and compare these electrodes for a structural job: strength, positions, polarity, hydrogen, handling and storage.
essays.modelAnswer: In both, E means electrode. The first two digits give the minimum tensile strength of the weld metal in thousands of psi: 70 000 psi (about 480 MPa) for E7018 and 60 000 psi (about 410 MPa) for E6013. The third digit, 1, means both can be used in all positions. The last digit gives the coating and current: 8 is a low-hydrogen iron powder coating, used on DCEP or AC; 3 is a rutile coating, used on AC or DC of either polarity. E6013 is easy to strike, gives a smooth, neat bead with easy slag removal, and suits light general work and thin sections. E7018 is stronger and its weld metal is tougher and very low in hydrogen, so it is the usual choice for structural steel, thick sections and restrained joints, where hydrogen cracking is a risk. It is harder to strike and needs a short arc. E7018 must be kept dry: stored in sealed packs or a heated oven, then a quiver, and re-dried as the maker says if it gets damp. E6013 should be kept dry too, but it is not as sensitive. For a structural job, E7018 is normally used, as the WPS says.
markingPoints: Explains E and the strength digits for both
Explains the position digit (all positions)
Explains the coating and current digit (low hydrogen DCEP/AC; rutile AC/DC)
Compares use: E6013 general and easy; E7018 structural, tough, low hydrogen
Storage: E7018 kept in oven or quiver and re-dried as the maker says

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare and set up MMAW work stations for a team welding a large frame on site. Include the power supply, cables, return path, VRD, duty cycle and the work area.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the site's supply: the voltage (110 V or 220 V) and outlets match the machines, there is RCD or other protection as the Centre's rules say, or I arrange an engine-driven welder placed outdoors with its exhaust away from people. I check each machine's rating and duty cycle against the current and the welding time we expect, so it does not overheat, and I make sure the VRD is working where the area is damp or confined. I check every cable, holder and clamp for damage, and choose cables big enough for the length and current, so voltage drop and heating are kept down. Cables are run where they will not be driven over or tripped on. The work clamp is fixed on clean metal close to each joint, so current does not stray through bearings, chains or other parts. I set up screens round each station, clear anything that can burn, put extinguishers near each one, and make sure there is ventilation. Each welder has dry PPE and a dry place to stand. I brief the team before work starts.
markingPoints: Checks supply voltage, protection or engine-driven set placed safely
Checks duty cycle and VRD
Checks cables, holders and clamps; cable size for length; safe routing
Work clamp close to the joint on clean metal; no stray current
Screens, fire precautions, ventilation, dry PPE and a team briefing

essays.stem: Explain the special hazards of acetylene and how each one is controlled when setting up oxy-acetylene equipment.
essays.modelAnswer: Acetylene is a highly flammable gas that can become unstable and decompose explosively if its pressure is too high, so it is never used above about 1 bar (15 psi) working pressure, and the regulator is set to the maker's chart for the nozzle. It is stored dissolved in acetone in a porous filling, so cylinders are kept and used upright; if one has been lying down, it is stood up and left before use, as the supplier says, so liquid acetone is not drawn out. Taking gas out too fast can also draw out acetone, so large nozzles use a manifold of several cylinders. Acetylene can form explosive compounds with copper and silver, so only fittings made for acetylene are used, never copper pipe. A flashback can travel back up the hose, so flashback arrestors and non-return valves are fitted, hoses are purged before lighting, and the correct lighting and shut-down order is followed. Leaks are found with an approved fluid, never a flame. A cylinder that gets hot or catches fire is an emergency: clear the area and call the fire service.
markingPoints: Pressure limit about 1 bar (15 psi); regulator set to the chart
Stored in acetone: cylinders upright; withdrawal rate and manifolds
No copper or silver-rich fittings
Flashback arrestors, check valves, purging, correct lighting order
Leak testing with approved fluid; emergency action for a hot cylinder

essays.stem: Describe the full pre-use checks, assembly, leak test and purge of an oxy-acetylene set for a team, and explain what the flashback arrestors and non-return valves do.
essays.modelAnswer: I check that the cylinders are upright and chained, in date and correctly labelled, and that the valve outlets are clean and free of oil and grease; I crack each valve briefly to blow out dust, standing to one side. I check that each regulator is for the right gas, undamaged, with its adjusting screw wound out, and fit it with the correct thread. Flashback arrestors are fitted at the regulator outlets, and non-return valves at the torch, or as the maker says. I check the hoses for cuts, burns and cracks, and fit them with the right connectors. I open the cylinder valves slowly, the acetylene key left on, and set the working pressures. With the torch valves shut, I brush an approved leak detection fluid on every joint and watch for bubbles; any leak is shut off and fixed. Then I purge each hose separately, in open air, to clear any mixed gas. A non-return valve lets gas flow only forward and stops gas flowing back into the other hose. A flashback arrestor also stops a flame travelling back to the regulator and cylinder, and many have a cut-off that shuts if they get hot.
markingPoints: Checks cylinders, valve outlets (no oil), cracking with care
Checks and fits regulators, arrestors, non-return valves and hoses correctly
Opens valves slowly and sets pressures to the chart
Leak tests with approved fluid and purges each hose separately
Explains non-return valve (stops back flow) and flashback arrestor (also stops a flame)

essays.stem: Explain how the bevel angle, root face, root gap and backing affect a butt weld, and the risks if each is wrong. Include a calculation for a single-V in 12 mm plate.
essays.modelAnswer: The bevel angle gives the electrode room to reach the bottom of the joint and fuse the sides. Too small an angle can cause lack of side-wall fusion and trapped slag; too large an angle wastes weld metal and time and increases distortion. The root face is the flat land left at the bottom of the bevel. Too thick and the root will not penetrate fully; too thin and the edges burn away. The root gap lets the root run penetrate through to the back. Too small gives incomplete penetration; too large gives burn-through and a sagging root. A backing strip supports the root when full penetration is needed from one side. For example, 12 mm plate with a 30° bevel and a 2 mm root face has a bevel depth of 12 − 2 = 10 mm. The top width of each bevel is 10 × tan 30° = 10 × 0.577 = about 5.8 mm, so with a 3 mm root gap the joint is about 5.8 + 5.8 + 3 = about 14.6 mm wide at the top. All these sizes come from the WPS and are checked with gauges at fit-up.
markingPoints: Bevel angle: access and fusion; too small or too large and the risks
Root face: too thick (no penetration), too thin (burns away)
Root gap: too small (incomplete penetration), too large (burn-through)
Backing supports the root for one-side full penetration
Correct calculation (10 mm depth, about 5.8 mm per bevel, about 14.6 mm total) and sizes from the WPS

essays.stem: Explain how hydrogen (cold) cracking happens in steel welds and how it is prevented while preparing for welding.
essays.modelAnswer: Hydrogen cracking needs three things together: hydrogen in the weld, a hard, brittle structure in the weld or the heat-affected zone, and stress. Hydrogen comes from moisture in electrode coatings, damp air, rust, oil, paint and condensation on the plate. Hard structures form when higher-carbon or alloy steels, or thick sections, cool quickly. Stress comes from shrinkage and restraint. The cracks can appear hours after welding, so they may be missed. To prevent it when preparing, I use low-hydrogen electrodes or processes as the WPS says, stored in an oven and quiver and re-dried when needed. I clean the joint and the area each side back to bright metal, removing rust, oil, paint and moisture. I preheat the joint to the temperature in the WPS, checked with a temperature crayon or thermometer, which drives off moisture and slows cooling, and I keep the interpass temperature in range. I design the fit-up to limit restraint, and plan the sequence. On some jobs, slow cooling or post-weld heating is used, and the WPS may require a delay before inspection.
markingPoints: Three causes: hydrogen, hard structure, stress
Sources of hydrogen (consumables, moisture, rust, oil, paint)
Low-hydrogen consumables stored and re-dried correctly
Cleaning, preheat and interpass control as the WPS says
Limits restraint; slow cooling or delayed inspection where required

essays.stem: Describe a plan to control distortion when preparing and welding a long steel frame or girder made from plate.
essays.modelAnswer: First I plan the joint design: the smallest weld size and bevel the drawing and WPS allow, and double-sided preparations on thick plate, because less weld metal means less shrinkage. I cut and fit parts accurately so gaps are not too big. I pre-set parts against the expected pull, for example setting a flange slightly out so that it pulls square, or pre-bending a girder slightly so it pulls straight. I tack the parts with tacks of the right size, evenly spaced and balanced each side, and use clamps, strongbacks or a jig to hold them, without making the joint so rigid that it cracks. I plan the welding sequence: weld from the centre outwards, balance welds each side of the neutral axis, and use back-step or skip welding on long seams, so heat is spread out. Where possible, two welders weld opposite sides at the same time. I keep heat input within the WPS. I check the frame for straightness and squareness after tacking and during welding, and record the results so the plan can be improved next time.
markingPoints: Reduces weld metal by joint design and accurate fit-up
Pre-sets or pre-bends against the expected distortion
Balanced tacking and restraint with clamps or jigs, without over-restraint
Planned sequence: centre outwards, balanced, back-step or skip
Checks and records straightness during the work

essays.stem: Describe the inspection a team leader carries out on the fit-up of a coded butt joint before welding, the gauges used, and what is recorded.
essays.modelAnswer: I check that the joint matches the drawing and the WPS. I confirm the material grade and heat number against the certificate and the parts list. I check the bevel angle with a bevel gauge or protractor, the root face with a rule or gauge, and the root gap with a gap gauge or feeler blades, all against the WPS ranges. I check hi-lo (misalignment) with a hi-lo gauge, especially on pipe, and the overall alignment and straightness with a straight edge. I check that the joint and the area each side are clean of rust, scale, paint, oil and moisture. I check the tack welds: their size and spacing, that they were made by a qualified welder, and that they have no cracks. I check that the right consumables are at the joint and stored correctly, and that preheat is ready if needed. Finally, I record each measurement, the gauges used, the result, the date and my name on the fit-up inspection sheet, and get it signed off by the inspector or supervisor before welding is allowed to start.
markingPoints: Checks against drawing and WPS; confirms material
Bevel angle, root face and root gap measured with suitable gauges
Hi-lo, alignment and cleanliness checked
Tacks, consumables and preheat checked
Records results, gauges, date and name; sign-off before welding

essays.stem: Explain how a hot work permit system works and the team leader's duties at each stage, from planning to sign-off.
essays.modelAnswer: A hot work permit is written permission to weld, cut or grind where there is a fire risk, given only after the area has been checked. In planning, the team leader looks at the job and the area and does a risk assessment: flammable materials, gas lines, nearby work, people, ventilation and how a fire would be fought. They apply for the permit from the person in charge. Before work starts, the area is prepared: combustibles removed or covered with fire blankets, gaps in floors and walls covered, extinguishers and a fire watch ready, screens put up and gas equipment checked. The permit is signed to show these checks are done, and it states the time limits and conditions, which the leader explains to the team. During the work, the leader makes sure the conditions are kept and stops work if anything changes. When the work ends, the fire watch stays for the time the permit sets, checking for smouldering material, including behind walls and below floors. Only then does the leader inspect the area, sign off the permit and hand it back to be kept on record.
markingPoints: Explains what a hot work permit is
Planning: risk assessment and applying for the permit
Preparation: combustibles, covers, extinguishers, fire watch, screens
During work: conditions kept and explained; stop if things change
After: fire watch for the set time, inspection, sign-off and record

practical1.title: Prepare and inspect fit-ups for a plate butt joint and a pipe butt joint to a written WPS
practical1.brief: As a team, prepare two joints for welding to the WPS the assessor gives you, as you would for a coded job: a single-V butt in two pieces of 12 mm carbon steel plate (about 300 mm × 125 mm), and a single-V butt in two short lengths of steel pipe. First, read the WPS and write a short preparation plan: the bevel depth and width (show the working), the root face and gap, the consumables, the preheat, the tools and who does what. Check the materials against the plan and the consumables in the electrode oven. Mark, cut and bevel the plates and pipe ends, grind the root faces, and clean back to bright metal. Set up an MMAW station and check it: cables, holder, clamp, polarity and current range for the electrodes, and the VRD where fitted. Set the root gaps with spacers or a line-up clamp, check the hi-lo, and have a member the assessor names make small, sound tacks to the WPS. Inspect both fit-ups with gauges and complete a fit-up inspection sheet for the assessor to sign. You do not need to weld the joints. Each member prepares at least one bevel and does at least one inspection check. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the joints and the inspection sheet are finished and the area is clean.
materials: 2 pieces of 12 mm carbon steel plate, about 300 mm × 125 mm
2 short lengths of steel pipe, as the assessor gives
Written WPS (from the assessor), plan sheet and fit-up inspection sheet
Oxy-fuel cutting set or bevelling machine, angle grinder with grinding disc, files
Bevel gauge or protractor, gap gauge or feeler blades, hi-lo gauge, steel rule
MMAW set, low-hydrogen electrodes from the oven, line-up clamp, spacers
photos: The written preparation plan with the bevel working
The bevelled plate edges showing the root face
The pipe ends bevelled and cleaned
The MMAW station set up and checked
Both fit-ups tacked, with gauges in place showing gap and hi-lo
checklist: Read the WPS correctly and worked out the bevel sizes
Checked materials and consumables against the plan and WPS
Prepared a bevel and root face within the WPS ranges
Cleaned the joint and the area each side back to bright metal
Set up and checked the MMAW station (cables, clamp, polarity, current, VRD)
Set the root gap and alignment; tacks small, sound and evenly spaced
Measured the fit-up with gauges and recorded the results accurately
Wore the right PPE throughout and left the area safe and tidy
safety: Wear a face shield and safety glasses when grinding; check the disc and guard
Follow the Centre's hot work rules for cutting and tacking: screens, extinguisher, ventilation
Check that the electrode holder, cables and clamp are undamaged; keep PPE dry
Treat cut and tacked parts as hot; use tongs and mark hot work
Lift plate and pipe with team lifts or lifting aids
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Plan and set up a shared oxy-acetylene and MMAW work area under a hot work permit
practical2.brief: As a team, plan and set up a work area at the Centre for two jobs the assessor describes: oxy-acetylene welding of 2 mm sheet and MMAW welding of a small frame. First, write a risk assessment and fill in a hot work permit request, then give a five-minute toolbox talk to the class on the hazards and your controls. Move the oxygen and acetylene cylinders on a trolley, secure them upright, and check the valve outlets. Fit the regulators, flashback arrestors, non-return valves and hoses, set the pressures from the maker's chart for the nozzle you choose, leak test every joint with an approved fluid and purge each hose. Light the torch, set a neutral flame, then shut down in the order the maker and the Centre's rules give. Set up the MMAW station with screens and check the machine, cables, clamp, duty cycle and VRD. Lay out extinguishers and keep a fire watch. When the assessor says the work is over, keep the fire watch, inspect the area and sign off the permit. Each member leads at least one part of the set-up, and every member speaks in the toolbox talk. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the permit, checklists and talk notes are finished and the area is safe.
materials: Oxygen and acetylene cylinders on a trolley with chains
Regulators, flashback arrestors, non-return valves, hoses, torch and nozzles
Approved leak detection fluid, spark lighter, cylinder key
MMAW set with cables, holder and work clamp; welding screens
Fire extinguishers, fire blanket and signs
Risk assessment form, hot work permit form, set-up checklists
photos: The risk assessment and permit request
The team giving the toolbox talk
The cylinders secured upright, with regulators, arrestors and hoses fitted
Leak testing the connections with fluid
The MMAW station set up with screens and extinguishers
The signed-off permit and the cleared area after the fire watch
checklist: Helped write the risk assessment and permit request with sensible controls
Spoke clearly in the toolbox talk
Assembled the gas equipment correctly, with arrestors and non-return valves
Set pressures from the chart, leak tested and purged correctly
Lit, adjusted and shut down the torch in the correct order
Set up and checked the MMAW station and fire precautions
Kept the fire watch, inspected the area and completed the sign-off
safety: Keep oil and grease away from all oxygen equipment; never use oxygen to blow dust or to ventilate
Keep acetylene cylinders upright and never set acetylene above about 1 bar (15 psi), or the Centre's lower figure
Leak test with approved fluid only, never a flame
Wear the right PPE: filter lenses of a suitable shade for each process, gloves, jacket and boots
Keep extinguishers at hand and a fire watch after the work, for the time the Centre's rules set
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
